tagline.text: A Spanish-era underground reservoir from 1882 beneath a San Juan shrine

location.label: Location
location.text: Inside the Pinaglabanan Shrine grounds, San Juan, Metro Manila (Pinaglabanan Street, Corazon de Jesus)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (free admission; transport and snacks, per person)

children.text: This museum, run by the NHCP inside the Pinaglabanan Shrine in San Juan, stands on top of a Spanish-era underground reservoir completed in 1882. In one visit you can learn Manila's waterworks history and the Katipunan's first battle, and even walk down into the reservoir tunnel.
Museo El Deposito is a history museum inside the Pinaglabanan Shrine in San Juan, Metro Manila. It is run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) and opened on
February 20, 2019
. The name "Depósito" is Spanish for storage tank, and it refers to the 19th-century underground reservoir directly beneath the building.
The reservoir was designed by the Spanish engineer Genaro Palacios and is part of the Carriedo Waterworks, built from
to

. It collected and treated water brought from the Marikina River, then sent it on to homes, public fountains and fire hydrants across Manila, including Intramuros. It is said to consist of one central channel joined by 25 smaller channels. The route of the water is also worth noting. The water reportedly came from the Marikina River through about
5 km
of cast-iron pipe passing near Santolan, and the system is described as large enough for about
300,000 people
. Capacity figures differ between sources, so treat the numbers as rough.
It took a long time for the reservoir to return to its present state. As water supply shifted elsewhere it lay neglected for decades, and in
a University of the Philippines archaeology team assessed and excavated it. In
the NHCP cleaned the tunnel, and according to Wikipedia the reservoir opened to the public on
November 30, 2021

. So the museum opened first and the reservoir followed. The museum is a two-storey building sitting on top of the reservoir. Inside are an audio-visual room, a resource center and a virtual reality room, and part of the reservoir's channels can be seen from inside the building. After the exhibits you can follow the staff down into the reservoir tunnel and walk through the dark stone space, an experience that is hard to find in other museums in central Manila.

The museum rarely appears in guidebooks, but it is a quiet and rewarding stop for Korean families in Manila and history-minded travelers. Admission is free, and if you combine it with the neighboring Katipunan museum and the Pinaglabanan Shrine, 1.5 to 2 hours is enough. Opening hours and tunnel access can change, so check the latest announcement before you go.

blocks.title: The underground reservoir tunnel beneath the building

children.text: The biggest attraction here is the underground reservoir. The stairs are wide at the top and narrow as you descend, and inside you will find stone walls, a high ceiling and dim lighting. A large central space leads to smaller compartments that were once filled with water. Which areas are open and how visits are guided depends on the day, so ask at the entrance. The tunnel smells of stone, and visitors describe it as either cool or hot, and only when you climb back up do you really feel that such a space lies under the middle of the city.

blocks.title: The Carriedo Waterworks and Manila's water story

children.text: The exhibits begin with how Spanish-era Manila got its water. Before piped water, people used rivers and creeks, or relied on water carriers who delivered it by the jar. The audio-visual room explains how this led up to the completion of the Carriedo Waterworks in 1882. You can also piece together the story that it began with a donation from the Spanish official Francisco Carriedo in 1733 and was finished almost 150 years later.

blocks.title: Artifacts from the reservoir and fire hydrants

children.text: The resource center holds items found while excavating the reservoir tunnel, such as bottles, along with old photographs, prints and scale models. A reconstructed fire hydrant stands next to an original one, so you can compare size and shape. Showing the waterworks through real objects is this museum's strength.

A miniature of the Carriedo Fountain is on display. It recalls the days when people in Manila collected water from public fountains. It is also a good way to explain to children how the water system began.

blocks.title: Battle of San Juan del Monte in virtual reality

children.text: The virtual reality room re-enacts the

Battle of San Juan del Monte, when the Katipunan tried to seize this reservoir. It is regarded as the first battle of the Philippine Revolution, so you can follow the story even without background knowledge. Check on site whether the room is operating.

The reservoir stayed in use after it stopped supplying water. It is said to have served as an armory during the American period and the Japanese occupation, and also as a pulmonary hospital for tuberculosis patients and as a firing range. It is interesting to see how one structure changed with each era.

blocks.title: The neighboring Katipunan museum and the shrine

children.text: Museo El Deposito stands within the Pinaglabanan Shrine grounds, with the Museo ng Katipunan next to it. They are separate buildings, but you can see both in one visit. You can also stroll around the shrine's monuments and park.

blocks.title: The 1972 historical marker and the park

children.text: A cultural property marker was installed at the reservoir site on August 30, 1972, and the surroundings became the Pinaglabanan Memorial Shrine and Park. The name Pinaglabanan means a place where people fought, and it comes from the 1896 battle. Knowing the origin of the name makes the exhibits easier to read.
Arrive when the museum opens. There may be a sign-in with your name and purpose of visit at the entrance, so follow the staff's instructions.
In the audio-visual room, watch the story of Manila's water before the Carriedo Waterworks.
In the resource center, take your time with the excavated artifacts, hydrants and the Carriedo Fountain model.
Follow the staff down into the reservoir tunnel. Looking around and taking photos usually takes about 20 minutes.
If the virtual reality room is running, try the Battle of San Juan del Monte.
Stroll the neighboring Katipunan museum and the shrine park, then head to Greenhills for lunch.

Opening hours are 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. per several sources (2024-2026). A last entry of 3:30 p.m. has been mentioned but is not confirmed by recent sources, so check on site. The museum is closed on Mondays, so plan your visit for Tuesday through Sunday.

items.title: Full-day route
items.subtitle: San Juan history walk and Greenhills

children.text: Enter Museo El Deposito and start with the audio-visual room and the resource center.
Look around the underground reservoir tunnel, then come up and rest in the shrine park in the daylight.
Continue with the stories around the revolution at the neighboring Katipunan museum.
Take a taxi or Grab to Greenhills for lunch.
Browse Greenhills Shopping Center or return to your lodging in the Ortigas area.
Because there is a last-entry time, it is safer to do the museum in the morning and the shopping in the afternoon.
Grab or a taxi from Ninoy Aquino International Airport, Makati or Intramuros is the simplest way. Depending on traffic, it can take
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
or more.
In a map app, search for "Museo El Deposito" or "Pinaglabanan Shrine".
Roads are very congested at rush hour. Travel during the daytime, when the museum is open.
Combining the MRT with a jeepney is described in some guides, but routes can change, so check locally.
From Greenhills Shopping Center, a taxi or Grab is the easiest.
The museum is inside the Pinaglabanan Shrine grounds, so you can walk to it from the entrance.
Since you will be inside the museum and the underground reservoir, rain does not matter much, but the dry season is more comfortable for walking in the shrine park and getting to the tunnel.
Underground it is humid, and visitors describe it as either cool or hot. It is an indoor route that avoids the midday sun, but bring drinking water.
The quietest time is right after opening. On weekdays around midday, school groups may crowd in and entering the tunnel can take longer.

rows: The most comfortable time for park walks and outdoor travel
A good indoor route, though some visitors say the underground is hot
Plan mostly indoor activities; travel takes longer in heavy rain

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
There are not many large hotels around the museum. Staying in Greenhills, Ortigas Center or Makati and taking a taxi is the easiest approach. The Ortigas and Makati areas are popular with Koreans.
Do not expect restaurants within the shrine grounds. Have lunch at a restaurant in downtown San Juan or the food court at Greenhills Shopping Center, and bring water with you.

If you miss Korean food, Korean restaurants are easy to find around Makati and Ortigas. After the museum, a simple Filipino meal or the Greenhills food court is a sensible choice. Business details change often, so check recent reviews in a map app.
The museum is closed on Mondays, so go from Tuesday to Sunday. Check the official NHCP announcement for exact hours before you visit.
A last entry of 3:30 p.m. has been mentioned but is not confirmed, so it is safer to arrive by 3 p.m. at the latest.
The stairs to the underground reservoir get narrow, so wear comfortable low-heeled shoes. One guide mentions hard hats being handed out at the entrance.
Visitor accounts recommend bringing a face mask, an extra shirt and drinking water.
For groups or school visits, it is best to reserve in advance through the museum's information page or contact address.
Planning the Katipunan museum and the shrine together means only one trip.
Ask at the entrance which areas allow photography and whether tripods are permitted.
Reading a short summary of Manila's waterworks and the 1896 Katipunan battle beforehand makes the exhibits much more enjoyable.
Allow at least 1.5 hours for the exhibits and the tunnel. A light visit to the museum takes about an hour, but including the tunnel and the neighboring museum adds more time.
Ventilation in the underground reservoir can be weak, and the guard at the entrance sometimes warns that gases may be trapped. If you feel dizzy, leave right away.
The tunnel is dark with stairs, so anyone with limited mobility or discomfort in enclosed spaces should check the situation at the entrance.
Opening hours, closing days and tunnel access can change, so check the latest announcement.
Do not touch the heritage structures or exhibits, and follow staff instructions.
In the rainy season the underground is very humid and the floor can be slippery.
If you bring children, hold their hands in the tunnel.
Official notices and visitor accounts list slightly different opening hours. Some older posts mention an 8 a.m. opening, so go by the official announcement.
This is the grounds where the museum stands. It has a park and monuments commemorating the
Battle of San Juan del Monte, where the Katipunan fought Spanish forces. You can walk around it. The battle, fought in late August 1896, is regarded as the first battle of the Philippine Revolution.
This NHCP museum right next to Museo El Deposito covers the history of the Katipunan revolution. It is good to visit together in the same grounds.
A nearby shopping and dining area. Travel time varies with traffic, so check locally.
A business and shopping district east of San Juan with many hotels and restaurants.
